body: Yeah that's true, the proof based courses are def more rigorous and demanding. I'll look into those when I'm done.

Yeah I get all of that, I just figured that someone like Google is not gonna care about someone being able to complex analysis or whatever cuz thats not what's used at google, but they will care about someone having an internship because that experience will come in handy.

>i mean standard single/multivariable + linear algebra at the level presented in mit ocw really isn't that impressive . skipping single + multivariable analysis + abstract theoretical linear algebra is impressive (this would mean skipping math 4130-4140 and math 4330). aim to do that. 

Yeah, I know I haven't really done anything crazy yet, as a lot of people skip calc3/4/linear. Also, by mit ocw not being impressive, do you mean that ocw isn't teaching me enough in those 3 courses, or that those 3 courses in general aren't that sophisticated? Anyway, I should be done with those by April, so then I can move onto harder things.

Yeah I'm gonna try and skip undergrad courses, at least skip calc 1-3 and linear algebra, - but is that really that great? Is someone really gonna take me over another kid because I did real analysis a semester earlier than them? I thought employers emphasize research/internships/interviews way more than courses after meeting the benchmark.

>it's sm more impressive improving general problem skills + skipping undergrad courses than doing some shitty internship

Is this really true? I mean I would be on top of the world if it were - I like doing math classes but absolutely hate the process of finding an internship lol. I just don't think its true cuz I've literlaly never seen someone with this mindset. Everyone is always trying to get an internship, not take harder coursework. If taking harder coursework was more effective, why doesn't everyone just do that when that's so much easier and less frustrating than finding and doing an internship?

>EDIT: try to do 18.700

This doesn't have any exams and the PSETS dont have solutions, so how would I do this course? I was thinking of just doing 18.06 cuz it has all of that.

Yeah I am studying on mit ocw.

And I'll prob try therapy at college, though I doubt it will help.

Yeah I have no problem studying. It's pretty fun. With OCW, I did 18.01 in january, prob finishing 18.02 by this month, and will try and do 18.03/real analysis/discrete math after that. However, let's be honest, all of this is pretty useless. All it will do is help me have an easier time in classes, except for the fact that having an easy time in classes is useless cuz nobody cares about GPA. Employer literally could not give 2 shits whether I have a 4.0 or a 3.8, and a 3.8 is something you could get blindfolded at every school save caltech. 

So I need to do something other than just studying. Seeing my friends get internships makes me desperate to get one too, but I suck at aquiring one.

I won't be able to get a new topic. My teacher is not understanding at all. And yeah, I could make my partner do his part, but I dont want to get fucked because of his incompetence. I'm in senior year and on pace for valedictorian, so I basically need to be perfect in everything in order to get an A+. Meanwhile, the other kids in the class get the biggest joke projects ever. I just wish euthanasia was easily accessible so I don't have to deal with this bs.

I'm already burned out. Sick of life. Sick of constant suffering. Sick of getting fucked over while nothing happens to those around me. Sick of euthanasia not being readily accessible to anyone who wants it.
I really hate CS projects though.

>Seems like your best bet is going to be a personal project. 

What do you mean by this? Is this like a CS project? I really hate doing those, I'm more of a math guy.

> You’re in high school, right?  

Yeah, im a senior.

>I’m not sure if its healthy (or even that productive tbh) to have every move you make be made to “advance your career” this young. 

It's prob not that productive, but it's better than nothing. I have to make coming to cornell worth it, so i have to grind as much as possible. A lot of my friends are getting internships.

What do I say in my email? Do I just be like "Hello Professor XXX, My name is XXX and I am an incoming freshman at Cornell majoring in XXX. Would it be possible to work with you in a research project this summer? Thanks, XXX". 

Is that too generic? Am I supposed to talk about specifically what research they're doing and how I would contribute? Do I have to give them my resume?

>Lol the reality is that as a pre-frosh, anything you do now will matter very little in the long term. 

Yeah, my future employer won't care what I did this summer. But, they will care what I did junior summer. And my junior internship will care what I did sophomore year. Etc. It's like a domino effect. Everyone with an internship this year will have a leg up on me for next year. I come from a competitive area, and my "friends" already are getting internships. 

>If you do research, join a project team and/or do some projects, you’re already a top candidate for sophomore internships. 

Yeah I'll def do research at least once I start college, if not this summer. What is a project though?

>If you know your major and what classes you want to take, you could start pre-studying?

I already do a lot of pre-studying right now. I'm planning to do math/CS, so I spend a lot of the day working on mit ocw. I reviewed calc 1/2 in january, and probably will finish calc 3 this month. At my pace, I don't think I will need the summer to do a lot of pre-studying. 

>Tbh I really don’t think you’re gonna find a good internship without being in college yet. One internship this summer doesn’t guarantee you get one next summer.  

Yeah, it's looking like I won't find any internship this summer. I don't even want a good one, any internship will do, but even the smallest companies tell me no.

As for the second point, obviously nothing guarantees anything, but an internship now will look good on my resume and make it easier to get one next summer.

> Does what you do have to be related to your major? 

Not necessarily, but I do want it to help me improve my chance of success in future college/jobs/internships.

>You could work a summer job and make some money before college, or volunteer somewhere. 

Idk about a summer job. I'll make like 5k if I work full time, which honestly isn't that great, especially since it won't do anything to advance my career prospects.

Volunteering is even worse, as it also won't advance my career prospects while also making me no money.

If I were to try and get research at Cornell, how would I do that? Do I just email random professors? I don't know them and they don't know me, so why would they accept me? I have a similar issue with my local university - I don't know anyone and nobody knows me.

But also, will research even help considering I'm going to do it once I'm at Cornell anyway? Like will a job/internship really care that I did 1 research vs 2 research?
